In your opinion, what is the best gin keeping in mind both taste and price? This would be for mixing. As a comparison to vodka, I think Smirnoff is a great tasting liquor in its price range, better than the bottom shelf stuff but not as expensive as Ketel One, etc.

Just as importantly, what is definitely a bad gin, something I shouldn't be caught dead drinking/serving?

I'm in USA, east coast, if that makes a difference to what's available.

As far as mid-range Gin goes, I'd suggest primarily using something like Beefeater or New Amsterdam - both are what I would consider mid-high ranging Gin. As for a truly excellent Gin, I'd recommend Hendricks - a distilled Scottish Gin, infused with Rose and Cucumber.

I hate to disagree with you, but in my opinion Smirnoff is one of the worse Vodkas - I'd prefer Svedka (a supposedly lower shelf vodka, made in Sweden.)

Thanks, I have had and enjoyed New Amsterdam, was wondering if there was anything better. Haven't tried Beefeater yet. I know Hendricks is cream of the crop, saving that for martinis! I've only begun to appreciate gin in the last year or so, it used to gross me out that it smelled like Christmas. I fell hard for Pimm's and gin was a short throw from there.

I never liked Svedka :/ but to each his own.

You can also check out Tanqueray and Bombay Sapphire - both are considered Top Shelf. People tend to be picky about their Gin though! I've never been a Gin drinker, but certain combinations really do work well! I once had a cocktail that was Hendricks Gin, St. Germain Elder Flower Liqueur, Lemon Lime Soda, Cucumber, and Lemon. The Cucumber and Lemon go in the glass first, followed by ice to the top of the glass. Then, you'll add 1.5 oz. Hendricks Gin, and 0.5 oz. St. Germain. At this point, you shake the ingredients rapidly 7-10 times; after which you'll top the glass off with the Lemon Lime Soda. Garnish with a Lemon Wedge, and Cucumber Slice, then Enjoy!

Gin is a funny one...

At the end of the day we are all talking about a spirit that is cheap as chips to make from the off casts of other spirits.

I get the feeling that Entry Level or mid range Gin in the UK and Europe is often seen as top shelf in the U.S. simply because of the branding.

I like Tanqueray as good ol' mid range gin, its ballsy and gives a solid Juniper hit that can shine through any cocktail slightly overpriced but oh well. TBH Gordon's is entry level but it does the trick just as fine, and it's produced pretty solidly. Unless you are having it in a martini, where you will miss that citrus and Bergamot.

Beefeater is considered entry level in the UK, It is respected and does the job fine though even if it can do with a higher abv (proof) imho, a decent rail gin no matter how you look at it.

Bombay Saphire is, or was at least, considered the boy band of gins in the scene that I was from, with a solid Bacardi marketing budget thrown behind it. It is good, but not bang for the buck. It's light easy flavour get's killed in almost everything you can smother it in. Bombay dry (the original) is actually pretty good though.

I'm not a big Hendrick's fan, it is a solid product but I find no practical use for it other than an effortless up sell to increase my bar turnover. It used to be pretty reasonable priced (10 years ago) but I think the price has gone up recently. I wont give an opinion here but I will say this: I can make any gin drink taste like fucking cucumber if I put enough of it in your glass.

Plymouth Gin is arguably my favourite go-to entry/mid range gin. It's priced well (in the UK) it has a decent balance of Juniper and fresh citrusy flavour, It has a solid abv (proof) to it that will not disappoint.

There was a craze about 5 years ago where every Tom, Dick, and Harry was making a "boutique artisian craft Gin", which was pretty novel for a while and some nice stuff came out of it. Some awesome stuff came out of it too but few. These brands will not be practical for this discussion over here.

Regarding what to stay away from is tricky but, and you probably know this, it is important to know that: "London Dry Gin" is not from London, it is a style of gin protected by law. So when in doubt, if it says "London Dry" you are safe, if it does not and it is cheap... you need to ask some serious questions.

I'd say stay away from your "no name" ones, with cheap gin you often need to find out the distillery where the alcohol was sourced from as it makes the difference. Find out what else they make there, and what the base spirit is. You don't want cheap ethanol mixed with juniper to be redistilled into something for consumption.

Edit: everyone here is so awesome, thanks! Yeah, I'm definitely calling it on needing new shoes. How often do you usually replace your running shoes?

Unless you've increased your mileage too much, too soon or you're running faster than normal, then yeah, it's probably the shoes. Easiest way to test it is to try running in a different pair of the same make/model/size with fewer miles on them. For me, I typically swap them out around the 200 to 300 mile mark. But I'm a big guy (~240 pounds) and usually beat the hell out of my shoes, especially when I first started running and had a heavy heel strike.

That is when I know to start looking at new shoes - when I begin to notice pain in my knee or foot. First few times it happened, I was like you and questioned if it was just me or what. Also, being a skeptic, I always thought of course the guy selling the shoes is gonna say replace them every 300 - 500 miles. Now that I have been running a while I have realized that 400 miles is about spot on for me. 
 I could definitely see shoes wearing out at 200 miles if 1) they are not high quality or 2) if you are a bit heavy.

It's probably the shoes--the 300-500 range is obviously huge and it depends on your weight, the surfaces you run on, your stride, etc. What I usually do is buy replacements and take them on shorter runs until they're broken in a little. If it's just the shoes you'll notice the difference pretty quickly!

I've heard all sorts of numbers about when to replace shoes and I suspect it varies between manufacturers. I do it mostly by feel. I find that my knees start to get more sore than usual on my long runs. Unfortunately, this method requires more understanding of how much you can run and how much your knees should hurt.

I'm a forefoot striker, so I don't get any joint discomfort from worn out cushioning in the shoes. As such, I guess they last a little longer with me. I replace shoes when the are worn out. Saucony shoes lasted the longest with me - 600 miles before the sole got worn out to the point where I was sliding along on wet asphalt. On the other end of the spectrum are Mizunos: 300 miles or so, and the first thing to go are the tops, inflection points, due to much thinner material.

I first noticed it about 3-4 months ago after intense runs, it would come on very mildly and usually not until the next day, last a day or two and leave, but it's been getting progressively worse after each run....even after taking breaks to let it heal.
